sentences.text: The name Pterodactylus translates to 'winged finger,' a fitting title for this extinct pterosaur.
This creature was a small pterosaur with an estimated wingspan of approximately 1.04 meters, much smaller than giants like Pteranodon.
Adult skulls were long and thin, holding about 90 narrow, conical teeth.
It is distinguished by having straight skulls and jaws, unlike the upwardly curved jaws of related ctenochasmatids.
The crest on the skull was composed mainly of soft tissue.
The genus was originally described by Georges Cuvier in 1809, with the type species being Pterodactylus antiquus.
The genus is thought to contain only this single species.
Many specimens previously attributed to P. antiquus based on soft tissue crest features have been reclassified as Aerodactylus scolopaciceps, which may be a junior synonym.
Pterodactylus was a generalist carnivore that likely ate various invertebrates and vertebrates.
Historically, different growth stages of Pterodactylus were often mistaken for distinct species.
Prince Charles Lucien Bonaparte established the family Pterodactylidae for Pterodactylus in 1838.
A 2017 analysis by Steven Vidovic and David Martill placed Pterodactylus as a basal member of the suborder Pterodactyloidea.
Fossils of Pterodactylus date to the Titoniense stage of the Late Jurassic, specifically the Tithonian stage, approximately 150.8 to 148.5 million years ago.
Fossils have been found primarily in the Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria, Germany, a diverse fossil site containing detailed imprints of soft-bodied organisms like jellyfish.
The classification of the group containing Pterodactylus has recently been subject to several competing definitions.

In 1996, Bennett suggested that differences between P. kochi and P. antiquus specimens could be explained by age differences, implying they are the same species. However, in 2014, Vidovic and Martill challenged the paradigm that P. kochi and P. antiquus were the same species.
Modern research has confirmed, refuted, or left disputed various assumptions about pterosaur biology, such as whether they were warm-blooded or furred.
